activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Raphael sat by the big window at the community centre. Miss Ada put two bowls of crackers on the table. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Raphael counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five." The last number was the same! He counted the second bowl. Six crackers there.

"This bowl has more," said Raphael. "Six is more than five." Miss Ada smiled and gave him a cracker.

His friend Sam dropped his cup. Ice fell out and sat on the table. Soon the ice began to melt into a little puddle. Raphael shared his crackers with Sam. One of Sam's crackers was broken in half, but it still tasted just fine.

"Can you count my crackers too?" Sam asked.

"Yes," said Raphael. "One, two, three."

story:
Nolan was at Grandpa's house. His hair had grown very long. It fell over his eyes. "Time for your first haircut," said Grandpa. "Hooray!" said Nolan.

They walked to the salon down the street. Nolan sat in a big chair. Grandpa stood right next to him. The hairdresser picked up her scissors. Click, click, click went the scissors.

Snip! A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. Snip! Another piece fell. The scissors cut, and the hair dropped. Nolan watched each piece fall. "More hair is falling!" he said. "It works!" said the hairdresser. "Every snip makes a piece fall."

Soon the cape was covered with hair. It looked soft and curly. The hairdresser brushed it all away. Now the cape was clean again. Nolan looked in the mirror. He could see his whole face! "I can see my eyes!" he said. Grandpa laughed. "You look so big," he said.

On the way home, Nolan found a piece of hair on his shirt. He held it up. "Look, Grandpa! One more snip fell!" Grandpa smiled. "We will show Grandma," he said. They hurried home fast. Nolan could not wait.

story:
Eliana sat on the soft rug. The living room was full of people. Grandpa sat in his big chair. Aunt Meg sat on the couch with a bowl of popcorn.

The big game was on TV. Everyone was shouting at the screen. Eliana could not see the TV at all. Uncle Ben's back was in her way.

Grandpa smiled at her. "Best seat in the house," he said.

"Where is the green?" Kai asked his teacher.

"Look in your cups and see," she said.

Kai dipped his brush in blue. He made a blue dot on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in yellow. He painted right on top of the blue dot. He rubbed the brush back and forth. The dot turned green!

Kai leaned close. "It changed!" he said. He sniffed the paint. It smelled like summer watermelons.

He made more dots. Red and yellow made orange. Red and blue made purple. The bad part was that his brush got mixed up. He washed it in the water cup. Then it was clean again.

Kai painted his frog all green. It had big eyes and a wide mouth. "Ribbit," said Kai.

His teacher smiled. "That is a fine green frog."

Kai zipped his brush back and forth one more time. The frog got greener and greener.

story:
Emile was at Grandma's house. It was time for dinner. Everyone sat at the big table. Grandma held up one hand. "We say our blessing first," she said.

Emile wanted to eat his noodles right now. But then he saw Grandma's hand. It was open, like a little hat. Papa put his hand on top. Mama put her hand on top too. The hands made a tall tower. Grandma smiled at Emile. "Your turn," she said.

Emile put his small hand on the tower. His hand was warm on top. "Thank you for our food," everyone said together. Emile said it too, in his small voice. Then Grandma poured juice into his cup. The tower of hands fell down with a plop. "All gone," said Emile. "Like magic," said Papa. Emile giggled and picked up his spoon.

Next she found a square sponge. She dipped it in white paint. She stamped it down. The square made the rabbit's body. Then she found a triangle stamp. One triangle made an ear. She stamped another triangle too. Now there were two pointy ears.

"Wash your hands first," said Mama. Sienna looked at her hands. They had dirt on them. Real dirt from the garden.

Mama turned on the water. Not too hot. Just warm. Sienna put her hands under it. Then came the soap. Bubbles! So many bubbles!

"Now we count," said Mama. "One, two, three." Sienna counted too. "Four, five, six!" She rubbed her hands together. The bubbles got bigger. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" They counted all the way to twenty.

Sienna looked at the bubbles. The dirt was gone! The bubbles had lifted the dirt away. Now her hands were clean and shiny.

"Look, Mama! The dirt went far away!"

Then Sienna showed her teddy bear. "Teddy needs soap too!" she said. She rubbed teddy's paws with bubbles. Teddy's paws got wet. Teddy got soapy all over!

"Teddy will dry on your bed," laughed Mama.

Sienna ate her apple slices. They tasted so good. Clean hands, sweet apples, and a soapy teddy waiting on the bed.

"Again tomorrow?" asked Sienna.

"Yes," said Mama. "Every single day."

story:
Mia was ready for bed. But her horse was missing. She looked under the bed. No horse. Mia felt sad. She wanted to hug her horse.

Daddy helped her look. Mia looked in the toy box. Only blocks. She started to feel angry. She put her hands on her hips. "Horse, where are you?" she asked. Then she listened. She heard a small sound. It came from the laundry basket.

Mia peeked in. There was her horse. She felt so happy. She hugged him tight.

Outside the window, soft snow was falling. Mia felt excited. "Daddy, will the snow cover the grass?" she asked. "Yes, by morning," he said. Mia felt scared of the dark for one little minute. Daddy held her hand. She felt calm again.

Mia tucked the horse under the blanket. "Night night, horse," she said. Her eyes closed, and she fell asleep.

story:
Grandpa came to stay at Harrison's house. He brought a big bag and his big shoes. Grandpa put the shoes by the door.

In the morning, Harrison could not find Grandpa. "Where is he?" Harrison asked Mom. Then Harrison heard a sound. Tappity tap. Tappity tap. It came from the hall. Harrison put one foot out of his room. The sound got louder. Grandpa was walking in his big shoes!

"There you are," said Harrison. He laughed and clapped his hands. "Your shoes go tap tap tap!"

"That they do," said Grandpa. He held out his hand. It was warm and soft.

All week, Harrison listened for the tap tap tap. When he heard it, he ran to Grandpa. One day Grandpa wore quiet socks. No tap came. Harrison looked and looked. Then he saw Grandpa's big feet under the kitchen table.

"Found you!" said Harrison. Grandpa lifted him up for a hug.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Kayden wanted to bake cookies with Grandma. Yesterday, the cookie jar was empty. Today, Grandma said, "We can bake now." Kayden jumped up and down.

First they had to mix the dough. Kayden poured in the sugar. He cracked one egg into the bowl. A little shell fell in, but Grandma fished it out. "You can try again later," she said. The second egg came out clean. Kayden smiled.

The dough had to sit in the fridge. "Now we wait," said Grandma. Waiting felt long. Kayden looked out the window. He saw a plane fly by. He waved at it. The plane was high and small, like a shy bird far away. "Is it cookie time now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Grandma. "Later, when the bell rings."

The bell rang at last. Grandma put the tray in the hot oven. Kayden stood back and watched. Soon the cookies were warm and golden. Grandma let one cool on a plate just for him. Kayden took a big bite. "We can bake more tomorrow," said Grandma. Kayden nodded, with crumbs on his chin.

Elizabeth was on the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to win the farm game called Five Senses. To win, she had to name each sense and the body part that goes with it.

Grandpa held up a red apple. Elizabeth closed her eyes. She could not see it. "My eyes see," she said. Then she sniffed the apple. "My nose smells apple pie!"

Grandpa laughed. "And the sheep wants a taste too." The black sheep nibbled her empty plate.

Grandma said, "We say a blessing together before we eat." She told Matteo he could hold the bread basket. Matteo held it with both hands. He walked very slowly. His elbow bumped a chair, but the basket stayed steady. A lady smiled at him.

Then everyone stood up. They held hands in a big circle around the table. Grandma held one of Matteo's hands. A boy on the other side held his other hand. "One, two, three," said the pastor. Then all the people said the blessing together. Their voices went around the table like a big warm hum.

After the blessing, everyone sat down. The bread basket was passed from hand to hand. Matteo watched each person take a piece. When the basket came back to him, he took one small piece for himself. "You held the bread," said Grandma. "That was a lucky job."

Matteo ate his soup and his bread. At the end, he helped stack the cups. Grandma said, "Same time next week?" Matteo nodded and picked up his crayon from his pocket. He drew a big table with many hands on the paper tablecloth.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Maverick planted tiny seeds in the dirt. He patted them down with his hands. "Now grow, little seeds," he said. Every day he came to the community garden. He looked and looked. But nothing grew. Just flat, dry dirt.

The sun made the ground hot and hard. Miss Ana pointed at the dry dirt. She poured water from a big can. Maverick watched the water sink in. The next day, the dirt was dry again. "The plants need a drink too," said Miss Ana. So Maverick got his own little can. He poured. He poured. He poured.

Soon a green sprout peeked out. Then two sprouts. Then three! One slip of water each day made more leaves come. Maverick counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." He watered again and smiled. "Grow, little seeds, grow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Eliana went to the store with Mama. Eliana held Mama's hand. "Stay close," said Mama. "One, two, my hand and you."

First they went to the bread corner. The oven there was big and hot. A man opened the door. Hot air puffed out. Eliana felt it on her face from far away. The man used a big pad to pull the bread out. "The pad helps him," said Eliana. "Yes," said Mama. "He is careful with hot things."

Next they stopped at the freezer. Eliana put one finger near the cold door. Brrr! It felt like ice. She pulled her finger back. "One finger, that is enough," she said.

Then Eliana saw a shiny knife on a low shelf. She reached out. Mama caught her hand right away. "We do not touch sharp things," said Mama. "We can look with our eyes." Eliana looked and looked. The knife was silver and long.

At the checkout, a kind woman gave Eliana a sticker. It had a doctor on it. The doctor was smiling. "The doctor helps people who get hurt," said Eliana. "Yes," said Mama.

At home, Eliana helped Mama clean the table. She wiped it with a cloth. One, two, three wipes. The table was clean. Then Eliana washed her hands. The water started cold. Mama turned the tap, and warm water came. Eliana held her hands under it.

"One finger in the freezer, two hands in the warm water," said Eliana. Mama smiled and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Emilia ran to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so she could not come. Today the sun was out and the sky looked beautiful.

"I want to swing," she said. But the swing was wet. Daddy touched it with his hand. "Wet now," he said. "It will dry later." Emilia stood by the swing and waited. Would it dry? She touched it too. Still wet. She touched it again. Not so wet now! The warm sun was doing it. The sun made the swing dry.

"Now it's dry!" she said. Daddy helped her onto the swing. She went up and down, up and down. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "Tomorrow we will come again."

A duck walked by the pond. "Where is the duck going?" Emilia asked. "Maybe to find lunch," said Daddy. The duck walked into the water. Emilia laughed and kicked her feet high. "See you tomorrow, duck!" she called.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Grayson walked on the nature trail with his dad. He wanted to solve a puzzle. The puzzle was about his five senses. He had to name them all.

First he saw a purple flower. "I see it with my eyes," he said. Then he heard a bird. "My ears heard that!" A pine needle felt prickly. "My hands tell me it is sharp." He sniffed the air. "My nose smells pine."

"One more," said Dad. Grayson thought hard. Dad gave him a small cracker from his pocket. Grayson ate it. "My tongue tastes it," he said. "That is five!"

They walked to the big oak tree. Grayson put his hand on the bark. He closed his eyes. "I can still feel it," he said. "Hands work in the dark too!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Hannah sat by the window on the big train. Her teddy sat on her lap. "We are going on a trip," said Mama. "We will sleep somewhere new tonight."

The train began to move. Hannah watched out the window. The station slid away. Trees went by, fast and slow. Then Hannah saw a field. A pink pig stood in the grass. Hannah tapped the glass. The pig ran. Its little legs went pitter, patter. The running pig made the mud splash up. Hannah laughed.

Mama held out a rice cake. Hannah took a small bite. Outside, another field came. The same pink pig? No, a brown cow. The train went faster. The cow got small, then it was gone. Hannah waved. "Bye, cow."

The train went into a tunnel. The window turned dark. Hannah held her teddy tight. Then the light came back. The window was bright again. Hannah saw hills and sheep. She shut her eyes, then opened them wide. The sheep were still there.

"Look, Mama," said Hannah. She pointed at the window. "Sheep!" Mama smiled and looked too. The train puffed on and on, all the way to their trip.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Lydia stood in the reading corner. A big red chair sat there. A shelf held books about bears and frogs.

The librarian said, "Here is your first library card." Lydia held it with both hands. She picked a book about a little red fox. "This one is mine," she said. "Mine forever and ever."

"You can take it home," said the librarian. "But you bring it back next week. Then other kids can read it too."

Lydia hugged the book tight. "But I love the fox," she said.

At home, Lydia read the fox book six times. Then Mama read it to her two more times. Lydia clapped when the fox found his den.

Next week, Mama took Lydia back to the library. Lydia gave the book to the librarian. She felt a small sad spot in her tummy.

Then a boy took the fox book off the shelf. He sat in the big red chair. He laughed at a funny page.

Lydia whispered, "He likes the fox too." She picked a new book about a frog. "This one is mine for now," she said.

The librarian smiled. "For now," she said. "And there is a song at story time next."

"Can we clap at story time?" asked Lydia.

"We always clap," said the librarian.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
It was sharing day at school. Weston brought his toy box to show. But when he opened it, the box was all mixed up. Cars sat with bananas. A sock sat with his teddy bear. Weston wanted to sort it all out.

His friend Mia came to help. "Let's make piles," she said. They put the toy animals in one pile. The cow went in. The pig went in. The duck went in. Soon the pile was full.

Next they made a food pile. Apples went in. Crackers went in. Then Weston saw something odd. A toy dog was in the food pile. "That does not fit," said Mia. Weston moved the toy dog to the animal pile. It fit there just right.

Then Weston heard a sound. Tap, tap, tap. He stopped to listen. A real class turtle was walking across the floor. The teacher picked it up. "Where does the turtle go?" she asked. Weston laughed. "Not in the food pile!" He pointed at the animal pile. "Right there, with the duck."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Sofia went to the library with Mama. She wanted a book about trucks. But she could not find one.

Then Sofia saw a circle on the rug. She stood on the circle. She clapped her hands. The clapping made a loud sound. A boy looked up from his square book. He held up a green truck book. "Is this the one?" he asked.

"Yes!" said Sofia. "Thank you."

The boy had a loose tooth. It wiggled when he smiled. "Can you wiggle it again?" Sofia asked. He did. She laughed.

They sat at the rectangle table. It had triangle flags on it. They read the truck book together. The wheels on the trucks were circles too. Then the library lady sang a song. Sofia and the boy clapped along.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Eleanor sat at the table. She wanted spaghetti for dinner. But Mom said, "Not today."

"Yesterday we had spaghetti," Mom said. "Today we are having soup." Eleanor looked into her bowl. It was warm and orange. She puffed out her cheeks. She wanted to be brave and try it.

"Now we fold our napkins," said Mom. Eleanor folded her napkin into a small square. Then she folded it again. It got smaller and smaller. "I folded it four times!" she said.

Eleanor took one little sip of soup. It tasted like carrots. She took another sip. Then a big sip. "Soup is good," she said. Mom smiled.

"After dinner we will wash the bowl," Mom said. "And later, it will be bedtime." Eleanor looked out the window. The sky was turning pink. "And tomorrow?" she asked. "Tomorrow," said Mom, "you can help me pick dinner."

Eleanor clapped her hands. "Spaghetti tomorrow!" she said. She picked up her spoon and took another big sip. Then she folded her napkin one more time and put it under her bowl.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Madeline went to the park with her dad. She wanted to find colors for her picture. "One, two, three, four," she said. She needed red, blue, yellow and green.

First she looked at the big tree. The leaves were green. "Green!" said Madeline. She pointed up high. She could not reach a leaf. Then the wind blew. One green leaf fell down. Madeline picked it up. The wind gave her the green leaf.

Next she saw the swing. The seat was blue. "Blue!" said Madeline. She sat on the swing. Dad pushed her up high. She held on tight. She jumped off and landed in the soft sand. Now she wanted red and yellow too.

She looked all around. She saw red roses by the bench. She picked up one red petal from the ground. "Red!" she said. Then she saw a yellow ball rolling near the slide. A boy threw it back to his friend. The yellow ball rolled to Madeline's feet. She touched it. "Yellow!" she said.

Madeline put her green leaf, red petal and a yellow flower Dad picked on the ground. Dad folded a paper hat for her. Madeline said the colors again. "Green, red, yellow, and... blue!" She ran back to the blue swing. "I found them all," she said. "Colors, colors, everywhere."
